summary: Motion means an object changes its position over time. We describe motion using distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration. Distance and speed are scalars; displacement, velocity and acceleration are vectors, which means they carry direction. Motion can be uniform or accelerated, and graphs of distance against time make these quantities easy to read. This page builds each idea slowly with small examples.

claims.statement: Motion is the change in position of an object with time.
Distance is the total path length and is a scalar; displacement is the shortest straight-line change from start to end and is a vector.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity and its SI unit is m/s2.
If a body starts from rest and gains a speed of 10 m/s in 5 s, its acceleration is 2 m/s2.
Average speed is total distance divided by total time; for example 100 m covered in 20 s gives an average speed of 5 m/s.
The slope of a distance-time graph gives the speed of the object.
Displacement and velocity are vector quantities because they carry direction.

key_terms.definition: the shortest straight-line distance from the starting point to the final point, together with its direction
speed in a particular direction; the rate of change of displacement
the rate of change of velocity with time
motion in which the object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time

equations.description: final velocity from initial velocity u, acceleration a and time t

misconceptions.wrong_belief: distance and displacement are always equal
misconceptions.correction: they are equal only when the path is a straight line with no turning back
